quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009f-01.title: Complements to a maximal subgroup
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009f-01.body:
**(a)** Let $X\in\mathfrak X$. Since $X\ne1$ and $X\cap H=1$, $X\not\le H$, so $HX$ is a subgroup (as $X\trianglelefteq G$) properly containing $H$; by maximality $HX=G$. Then $|G|=|H||X|/|H\cap X|=|H||X|$, so $|X|=|G:H|$ for every $X\in\mathfrak X$. If $1\ne Y\le X$ with $Y\trianglelefteq G$, then $Y\cap H\le X\cap H=1$, so $Y\in\mathfrak X$ and $|Y|=|G:H|=|X|$, giving $Y=X$. So $X$ is minimal normal.

**(b)** Let $X\in\mathfrak X$ be abelian and $p$ a prime dividing $|X|$. $\Omega=\{x\in X\mid x^p=1\}$ is a subgroup ($X$ abelian), nontrivial (Cauchy) and characteristic in $X$, hence normal in $G$; by minimality $\Omega=X$. So $|G:H|=|X|=p^k$. Any $Y\in\mathfrak X$ has order $p^k$, so it is a $p$-group; its center $Z(Y)\ne1$ is characteristic in $Y$, hence normal in $G$, so $Z(Y)=Y$ by minimality and $Y$ is abelian.

**(c)** $U\cap V$ is normal in $G$ and lies in $U$; by minimality it is $1$ or $U$, and $U\cap V=U$ would give $U\le V$, so $U=V$ by minimality of $V$. Thus $U\cap V=1$, $[U,V]\le U\cap V=1$, and $UV=U\times V$. Put $D=UV\cap H$; since $UV\trianglelefteq G$, $H$ normalizes $D$. Let $W\in\mathfrak X\setminus\{U,V\}$; as before $W\cap U=W\cap V=1$ and $W$ centralizes $U$ and $V$. Recall $G=HU=HW$ from (a).

*Case 1: $U$ abelian.* By (b) $V$ is abelian, so $UV$ is abelian and $U$ centralizes $D\subseteq UV$. Since $H$ and $U$ normalize $D$, $D\trianglelefteq HU=G$.

*Case 2: $U$ nonabelian.* $W\cap UV$ is normal in $G$ and contained in $W$, so it is $1$ or $W$. Suppose $W\le UV$. The projection $\pi\colon U\times V\to U$ restricted to $W$ has kernel $W\cap V=1$, so it is injective. For $w=uv\in W$ ($u\in U$, $v\in V$): $w$ and $v$ both centralize $U$, hence so does $u=wv^{-1}$, i.e. $u\in Z(U)$. Thus $|W|\le|Z(U)|<|U|$, contradicting $|W|=|U|$ from (a). Therefore $W\cap UV=1$, so $[W,UV]\le W\cap UV=1$ and $W$ centralizes $D$. Since $H$ and $W$ normalize $D$, $D\trianglelefteq HW=G$.

*Conclusion.* $D\trianglelefteq G$ and $D\cap U\le H\cap U=1$, so $[D,U]\le D\cap U=1$; likewise $[D,V]=1$. Hence $D$ centralizes $UV$, and as $D\le UV$, $D\subseteq\mathbf Z(UV)$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009f-02.title: Integral extensions and fields
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009f-02.body:
**(a)** Let $s\in S$ with $rs=1$. Since $s$ is integral, $s^n+a_{n-1}s^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0=0$ for some $a_i\in R$, $n\ge1$. Multiplying by $r^{n-1}$ and using $rs=1$ gives $s+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}r+\cdots+a_0r^{n-1}=0$, so $s\in R$.

**(b)** Choose a monic $m(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0\in R[x]$ of minimal degree $n\ge1$ with $m(s)=0$. If $a_0=0$ then $s\,q(s)=0$ with $q(x)=x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1$, so $q(s)=0$ by regularity. If $n\ge2$ this contradicts minimality; if $n=1$ it says $1=0$, so $S=0$ and there is nothing to prove. Hence $a_0\ne0$, which is invertible in the field $R$, and
$$s\cdot\big(-a_0^{-1}(s^{n-1}+a_{n-1}s^{n-2}+\cdots+a_1)\big)=-a_0^{-1}(m(s)-a_0)=1.$$

**(c)** Let $\mathfrak p=R\cap P$, a prime ideal of $R$. The map $R/\mathfrak p\to S/P$ is injective (its kernel is $(R\cap P)/\mathfrak p=0$), so $A=R/\mathfrak p\subseteq B=S/P$ are integral domains with the same $1$, and $B$ is integral over $A$ (reduce an integral equation modulo $P$). We show: $A$ is a field iff $B$ is a field.
- If $A$ is a field and $0\ne b\in B$, then $b$ is regular ($B$ is a domain), so $b$ is invertible by (b).
- If $B$ is a field and $0\ne a\in A$, then $a^{-1}\in B$, so $a^{-1}\in A$ by (a).

Hence $P$ is maximal $\iff$ $S/P$ is a field $\iff$ $R/\mathfrak p$ is a field $\iff$ $R\cap P$ is maximal. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009f-03.title: Tower law with $F(\alpha^n)\subseteq F(\alpha)$
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009f-03.body:
**(a)** Since $f$ and $g$ are irreducible, $[F(\alpha):F]=\deg f$ and $[F(\alpha^n):F]=\deg g$. From $F\subseteq F(\alpha^n)\subseteq F(\alpha)$,
$$\deg f=[F(\alpha):F(\alpha^n)]\cdot\deg g,$$
so $\deg g\mid\deg f$. Moreover $\alpha$ is a root of $x^n-\alpha^n\in F(\alpha^n)[x]$, so $\deg f/\deg g=[F(\alpha):F(\alpha^n)]\le n$.

**(b)** If $\alpha=0$ then $f=x$ (up to a constant), $\deg f=\deg g=1$, $n=1$ and $1\in E$ is a primitive first root of unity. Assume $\alpha\ne0$ and put $K=F(\alpha^n)$, $c=\alpha^n\neq 0$. Now $[F(\alpha):K]=n$, so the monic polynomial $h(x)=x^n-c\in K[x]$, of degree $n$ with root $\alpha$, is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $K$. Since $f(\alpha)=0$ and $f\in K[x]$, $h\mid f$ in $K[x]$; as $f$ splits over $E\supseteq K$, so does $h$.

Since $\operatorname{char}F\nmid n$ and $c\ne0$, $h'=nx^{n-1}$ has only the root $0$, which is not a root of $h$; so $h$ has $n$ distinct roots $\alpha_1=\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n\in E$. The ratios $\alpha_i/\alpha$ are $n$ distinct $n$th roots of unity in $E$. Thus the group $\mu_n(E)$ of $n$th roots of unity in $E$ has exactly $n$ elements; as a finite subgroup of $E^\times$ it is cyclic, and a generator is a primitive $n$th root of unity. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009f-05.title: Divisibility and essential subgroups
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009f-05.body:
**(a)** Let $\phi\colon A\to\bar A$ be a surjective homomorphism, $\bar a\in\bar A$ and $n\ge1$. Write $\bar a=\phi(a)$ and choose $b\in A$ with $b^n=a$. Then $\phi(b)^n=\phi(a)=\bar a$.

**(b)** Let $n=|A|$. For $a\in A$ choose $b$ with $b^n=a$; by Lagrange $b^n=1$, so $a=1$. Hence $A=1$.

**(c)** Suppose $B\ne A$ and pick $b\in B\setminus A$. Let $m$ be the least positive integer with $b^m\in A$; it exists, since $\langle b\rangle\ne1$ gives $\langle b\rangle\cap A>1$, i.e. $b^k\in A\setminus\{1\}$ for some $k\neq 0$, and we may take $k>0$. As $b\notin A$, $m>1$; let $q$ be a prime dividing $m$ and replace $b$ by $b^{m/q}$. Now $b\notin A$ (by minimality of $m$) but $b^q\in A$.

Since $A$ is divisible, there is $c\in A$ with $c^q=b^q$. Put $b'=bc^{-1}$. Then $b'^q=1$ and $b'\notin A$ (else $b=b'c\in A$); in particular $b'\ne1$, so $\langle b'\rangle$ has prime order $q$. By hypothesis $\langle b'\rangle\cap A>1$; a nontrivial subgroup of a group of prime order is the whole group, so $\langle b'\rangle\le A$ and $b'\in A$ — a contradiction. Hence $A=B$.

(Alternatively: divisible abelian groups are injective $\mathbb Z$-modules, so $B=A\times C$ for some $C$; then $A\cap C=1$ forces $C=1$.) ∎
